      • This is a prototype built only from public data.
      • Buses are not included, so the train's benefit may look bigger than it really is.
      • The "money still missing" is a range from news reports, not an official figure.
      • The legal points need a lawyer to confirm. Sound Transit can't charge homeowners itself; the City of Seattle would have to.

      Please read before relying on these numbers

      • This is a prototype. It was built only from public data, not with Sound Transit or the City of Seattle. It is not official advice.
      • The price result is not very reliable. It passed only some reliability checks. Read it as "no clear rise", not "prices fell".
      • Buses are not included. Travel times use walking and trains only, so the train's benefit may look bigger than it really is.
      • The "money still missing" figure is not official. It is a range from news reports. A firm agency figure would replace it.
      • Legal points need a lawyer. Sound Transit cannot charge homeowners itself; the City of Seattle would have to.
      • Building heights are partly estimated. About 2% are measured. The rest come from the number of floors, Microsoft's computer estimate, or a standard 6 m.
      • The 3D trains are an illustration. They do not follow the real timetable. They are drawn wider than real so they are easy to see, and they move faster when you zoom out.
      • The West Seattle line's route is not final. The dashed line simply joins the planned stations.
      • The year slider shows today's track. It only lights up stations and areas as they open; the lines themselves are always drawn.
      • Where people live is approximate. Household figures are averages for each neighbourhood, not for individual homes.

      From raw data to answer, step by step. Technical names are in grey.

      1. Collect the facts. Every house sale in King County from 1995 to 2026, the date each Link station was paid for and opened, and the street and footpath network.
      2. Measure walking distance. Walking time from every property to the nearest station, along real streets at 80 metres a minute. Under 10 minutes is "close"; 20–40 minutes is the comparison group; homes in between are left out.
        Network walking time with Dijkstra's shortest paths on the OpenStreetMap network
      3. Measure how much the train helped. Jobs reachable within 45 minutes by walking and train, each year. The jump when a station opens is the "access gain".
        Cumulative-opportunity accessibility from LODES 2019 jobs; buses not modelled
      4. Compare before and after. Price changes of close homes against comparison homes, before and after each station was funded. House size, age, condition and neighbourhood are accounted for, so like is compared with like.
        Difference-in-differences with staggered timing (Callaway and Sant'Anna 2021), doubly robust, not-yet-treated controls; 999-draw cluster bootstrap
      5. Turn it into a rate. Each station's price change divided by its access gain: how much more homes are worth per unit of better access.
        Price elasticity with respect to accessibility, weighted across stations
      6. Test the result. Seven checks, such as planting a fake price rise to see if the method finds it, and fake stations and dates where no effect should appear. The result passed only some.
        Falsification suite: planted effect, pre-trend bounds, placebo stations, placebo date, composition, leave-one-station-out, rezoning split
      7. Apply it to West Seattle. The access gain from the two new stations, the value each nearby home would gain, and what a charge of 30–60% of that gain would raise over 20 years, in today's dollars. Repeated 10,000 times with different assumptions.
        Local improvement district and tax increment area revenue models; Monte Carlo simulation
      8. Decide. The answer goes through six yes/no checks, in order: legal, enough data, a clear price rise, reliable, enough money (5% of the gap), fair to households. It stops at the first "no".
        Decision gates G0–G5
      9. Rules written down first. All choices were locked before the results were seen, so they could not be bent. The one later change is recorded with its reason.
        Pre-analysis plan with a SHA-256 lock (docs/pre_analysis_plan.md, docs/decisions/)
